items.stem: What is a semantic field?
options: The order of words in a sentence
The sound pattern of a line
A list of synonyms in a dictionary
A group of words related by a shared area of meaning
items.answer: A group of words related by a shared area of meaning
items.markingKey: E.g. attack, defence, battle = a semantic field of war.

items.stem: Comment on the lexical and semantic choices in ‘a machine that breathed for him’ (a fundraising email from a children’s hospital charity) and their effect on the audience.
items.answer: Personification: the machine performing a basic human act emphasises how fragile the child was.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks: 1 mark – names or describes the feature accurately (personification, lexis and semantics); 1 mark – explains the effect: the machine performing a basic human act emphasises how fragile the child was; 1 mark – links the effect to the audience (past donors and potential charity runners) or purpose (to persuade readers to sign up for a fundraising run).

items.stem: This sentence comes from a magazine feature: ‘The building has three floors.’ Identify the lexical and semantic feature and explain its effect.
items.answer: Neutral: the sentence is factual with no evaluative lexis.

items.stem: Read Text A, a review from a city magazine’s food column. ‘Arrive hungry and leave your diet at home. The new night market on Harbour Road is loud, cramped and gloriously chaotic, and I loved almost every minute. The star is a tiny stall run by two sisters who fold dumplings so fast their hands blur; their pork-and-chive parcels (six for a very reasonable price) are worth the twenty-minute queue alone. The grilled corn was a disappointment – charred outside, oddly cold within – and seating is a battle you will probably lose. Still, for sheer energy there is nothing like it in the city. Four stars.’ Analyse how the writer uses lexis and semantics in this text. Refer to two examples and explain their effects.
items.answer: ‘fold dumplings so fast their hands blur’ – hyperbole: the exaggeration creates a vivid image of skill and speed, making the stall seem like a spectacle. ‘seating is a battle you will probably lose’ – metaphor: the comic war metaphor warns readers about crowding while keeping the tone light.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘fold dumplings so fast their hands blur’ (hyperbole): the exaggeration creates a vivid image of skill and speed, making the stall seem like a spectacle; ‘seating is a battle you will probably lose’ (metaphor): the comic war metaphor warns readers about crowding while keeping the tone light; ‘I loved almost every minute’ (hedging): ‘almost’ qualifies the praise, preparing for the criticisms and making the reviewer seem fair; or any other valid, supported point. Up to 1 mark for each accurate identification and up to 2 for each developed explanation of effect.

items.stem: Read Text A, a speech by a city councillor at a residents’ meeting launching a rooftop-garden scheme. ‘Friends, neighbours, fellow gardeners – thank you for coming out on such a wet evening. Look up when you leave tonight. Every flat roof you see is a field waiting to be planted. Last summer, the pilot garden on the bus depot grew four hundred kilos of vegetables, cooled the building below by three degrees and gave thirty families somewhere to meet. Imagine that on every block. Some say it is too expensive. I say we cannot afford not to. So I am asking you tonight: lend us your hands, your weekends and your stubbornness, and together we will turn this grey city green.’ Analyse the ways in which lexis and semantics and other language choices shape the meaning of this text.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘Every flat roof you see is a field waiting to be planted.’ (metaphor): unused concrete is reframed as fertile farmland; ‘waiting’ suggests the roofs are almost asking to be used; ‘grew four hundred kilos of vegetables’ (precise numerical detail): concrete figures from the pilot scheme give the speaker credibility and make the benefits measurable; other relevant features: ‘Friends, neighbours, fellow gardeners’ (tricolon); ‘Look up when you leave tonight.’ (imperative); ‘Some say it is too expensive. I say we cannot afford not to.’ (antithesis); ‘lend us your hands, your weekends and your stubbornness’ (tricolon); ‘turn this grey city green’ (alliteration); ‘together we will’ (inclusive pronoun).

items.stem: Read Text A, a news article from a national newspaper. ‘Reservoirs at Record Low as Heatwave Grips Capital. Water levels in the capital’s three main reservoirs have fallen to 31 per cent of capacity, the lowest figure since records began in 1978, officials confirmed yesterday. From Monday, the use of hosepipes and sprinklers will be banned, and car washes must recycle at least half of the water they use. “We are not yet in a crisis,” said Dr Leila Haddad, director of the regional water authority, “but every household can make a difference.” Forecasters expect temperatures to remain above 38°C for at least another week. Critics argue that the authority has failed to repair leaking pipes, which lose an estimated fifth of all treated water.’ Analyse how the writer uses lexis and semantics in this text. Refer to three examples and explain their effects.
items.answer: ‘Heatwave Grips Capital’ – personification: the dynamic verb ‘grips’ presents the heat as a physical force holding the city, adding drama to a factual report. ‘the lowest figure since records began in 1978’ – precise numerical detail: the historical comparison quantifies the seriousness and gives the report authority. ‘an estimated fifth’ – hedging: ‘estimated’ qualifies the figure, showing journalistic caution about an unverified statistic.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘Heatwave Grips Capital’ (personification): the dynamic verb ‘grips’ presents the heat as a physical force holding the city, adding drama to a factual report; ‘the lowest figure since records began in 1978’ (precise numerical detail): the historical comparison quantifies the seriousness and gives the report authority; ‘an estimated fifth’ (hedging): ‘estimated’ qualifies the figure, showing journalistic caution about an unverified statistic; or any other valid, supported point. Up to 1 mark for each accurate identification and up to 2 for each developed explanation of effect.

items.stem: Rewrite ‘Someone broke the window.’ in the passive voice, and explain why a writer of a news report that wants to sound impersonal might prefer the passive form.
items.answer: The window was broken. The passive shifts focus to the action or the thing affected and allows the agent to be omitted, which suits a news report that wants to sound impersonal.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: correct passive form; agent optional or omitted correctly; explains change of focus; links to the purpose of a news report that wants to sound impersonal.

items.stem: Read Text A, a feature article in a regional newspaper about the closure of the Rialto cinema. ‘For ninety-two years the Rialto has been the place where this town fell in love – with film stars, with stories, and quite often with each other. On Sunday its velvet curtains will close for the last time. Inside, the carpet is threadbare and the seats creak like old ships, but the projectionist, Mr Farouk, still climbs the narrow stairs each evening as he has done since 1979. “People say streaming killed us,” he shrugs. “Maybe. But you cannot laugh with three hundred strangers on your sofa.” The building will become a car park.’ Analyse the ways in which discourse and structure and other language choices shape the meaning of this text.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘“People say streaming killed us,”’ (direct quotation): the projectionist’s own words give a personal, authentic voice to the story; ‘The building will become a car park.’ (bathos): the flat final sentence deflates the nostalgia and implies criticism without stating it; other relevant features: ‘the place where this town fell in love’ (metaphor); ‘with film stars, with stories, and quite often with each other’ (tricolon); ‘its velvet curtains will close for the last time’ (metaphor); ‘the seats creak like old ships’ (simile); ‘you cannot laugh with three hundred strangers on your sofa’ (antithesis).

items.stem: Read Text B, an editorial in a national newspaper, ‘Pocket the Phones’. ‘The evidence is now difficult to ignore. In schools that have removed smartphones from the school day, teachers report calmer corridors, fewer incidents of online bullying and, in several studies, modest gains in test scores. Of course, a ban is not a cure-all; determined pupils will always find a way, and parents understandably want to be able to reach their children. But these are problems of management, not of principle. Children deserve a few hours each day in which their attention belongs to them rather than to an algorithm. Schools should pocket the phones – and keep them pocketed.’ Analyse how the writer uses phonology and prosody in this text. Refer to one example and explain its effect.
items.answer: ‘calmer corridors’ – alliteration: the /k/ alliteration makes the benefit memorable and suggests order.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘calmer corridors’ (alliteration): the /k/ alliteration makes the benefit memorable and suggests order; or any other valid, supported point. Up to 1 mark for each accurate identification and up to 2 for each developed explanation of effect.

I mean’ (discourse marker); ‘took my dog out’ (idiom); ‘I: on the pavement’ (echoing).

items.stem: Read Text A, a news article from a national newspaper. ‘Reservoirs at Record Low as Heatwave Grips Capital. items.stem: Read Text A, a feature article in a regional newspaper about the closure of the Rialto cinema. ‘For ninety-two years the Rialto has been the place where this town fell in love – with film stars, with stories, and quite often with each other. On Sunday its velvet curtains will close for the last time. Inside, the carpet is threadbare and the seats creak like old ships, but the projectionist, Mr Farouk, still climbs the narrow stairs each evening as he has done since 1979. “People say streaming killed us,” he shrugs. “Maybe. items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘the place where this town fell in love’ (metaphor): the town is personified as a lover, presenting the cinema as the heart of the community; ‘its velvet curtains will close for the last time’ (metaphor): the closing curtains symbolise the end of an era, giving the closure theatrical finality; ‘the seats creak like old ships’ (simile): the comparison suggests age and romance, making decline seem dignified. (Transcription key: (.) micropause; (1) pause in seconds; // overlapping speech; CAPITALS = stressed word; [ ] non-verbal feature.) ‘P: and on line two we’ve got Samuel (.) morning Samuel C: morning (.) erm yeah I just wanted to say (.) items.stem: This text is a thread of comments posted under a local news website’s report on the Rialto closure, public comments posted online under a news report. Read Text B, a thread of comments posted under a local news website’s report on the Rialto closure. ‘@filmfan_88: Saw my first ever film there in 1996 😭 end of an era. | @nadia.k: Honestly? It was freezing and the sound was terrible. Nostalgia is fine but nobody actually WENT. | @filmfan_88: @nadia.k harsh but… fair 😂 | @localhistory: The Rialto opened in 1932 with a silent film and a live orchestra. Photos in our archive (link below). | @samuel_w: car park. a CAR PARK. unbelievable.’ Analyse the ways in which language and style are used in this text.
items.answer: Indicative content: overview of genre, audience (other readers of the local news website), purpose and context; ‘😭’ – emoji (graphology and visual design): the crying emoji conveys grief playfully, standing in for facial expression; ‘end of an era’ – cliché (lexis and semantics): the familiar phrase sums up the loss quickly, typical of informal online comment; ‘Honestly? It was freezing’ – rhetorical question (grammar and syntax): the one-word question announces a frank, contrary view; ‘nobody actually WENT’ – capitalisation for emphasis (graphology and visual design): capital letters mimic spoken stress and make the criticism forceful; ‘@nadia.k harsh but… fair 😂’ – social media handle (graphology and visual design): the handle addresses one commenter directly, creating a conversation within the thread; ‘car park. a CAR PARK. unbelievable.’ – repetition (discourse and structure): repetition, capitals and lower-case fragments convey disbelief and anger; ‘Photos in our archive (link below).’ – compressed noun phrases (grammar and syntax): the verbless phrasing and link are typical of informative online posts.
